title: New Zealand Signed a Trade Deal With India. Then It Quietly Started Writing Immigration Rules That Apply to Indians — and Only Indians.
excerpt: Even NZ's own Foreign Minister calls the proposed restrictions discriminatory. Days before Modi's first-ever visit, the country's coalition government is tearing itself apart over who gets to come in.
body:
In late April, India and New Zealand signed what both governments called a historic free trade agreement — the first comprehensive trade pact between the two countries. Within weeks, New Zealand's government began drafting immigration rules that single out Indian nationals for restrictions no other trade partner faces.

The revelation, made public by New Zealand's own Foreign Minister Winston Peters, has exposed a raw fracture inside the country's ruling coalition, raised accusations of racism, and injected deep unease into the Indian diaspora community just as Prime Minister Narendra Modi prepares for his first-ever official visit to New Zealand next week.

## 'India and India Alone'

Peters, the leader of coalition partner New Zealand First, dropped the bombshell during a parliamentary debate last week when he revealed that the government's Immigration Minister, Erica Stanford, had been developing new immigration settings that target India exclusively.

"We've recently received the evidence in the form of a briefing from officials and the consequent decisions made by the Minister of Immigration that immigration policy settings are being made more restrictive in a way which targets India and India alone," Peters told Parliament.

The proposed changes would impose a labour market and economic needs test on Indian nationals that doesn't apply to citizens of other countries with similar FTA arrangements. They would also preclude Indian citizens from applying for a temporary employment entry visa from within New Zealand — an option available to nationals of other trade partners.

"This is our concern as Foreign Minister, because they are potentially damaging to our reputation as a country that is transparent in dealings and one whose word can be relied upon," Peters said. "The government must explain why these restrictions will apply to India and India alone and not to all New Zealand FTA partners."

Immigration Minister Stanford confirmed that a draft of the proposed changes had been circulated to ministers but said no final decisions had been made. Officials, Peters noted, had warned that the more restrictive settings could damage bilateral and trade relations with India and potentially open New Zealand to legal challenge and retaliatory action.

## The 'Butter Chicken Tsunami'

The diplomatic tensions are playing out against a backdrop of increasingly ugly rhetoric. In April, just days before the FTA was signed in New Delhi, NZ First's deputy leader and Minister for Regional Development Shane Jones used a phrase that has become a lightning rod for the Indian community.



> **""National preferred doing a quick, low-quality deal over doing the hard work necessary to get a fair deal that delivers for both New Zealanders and Indians," he said."**


"I don't care how much criticism we get, I am just never going to agree with a butter chicken tsunami coming to New Zealand," Jones told Reality Check Radio, referring to projected Indian immigration under the trade deal.

The remark was condemned as racist by Indian community groups, opposition lawmakers, and commentators across both countries. Opposition MP Priyanca Radhakrishnan — herself of Indian origin — called it "outright racism." Shanti Patel, president of the Auckland Indian Association, said the language was "incredibly worrying for everybody."

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, while declining to label the comments racist, called them "unhelpful" and "alarmist." Jones defended his words as "hyperbole" used to "get cut through in debates."

But the damage extended beyond a single soundbite. Community leaders say the minister's comments normalised a climate where anti-Indian sentiment could be expressed openly. A BBC investigation found that a survey of New Zealanders showed significantly more welcoming attitudes toward British migrants compared to those from India, suggesting deeper structural biases.


![Prime Minister Narendra Modi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5f/The_official_portrait_of_Shri_Narendra_Modi%2C_the_Prime_Minister_of_the_Republic_of_India.jpg)


## What the FTA Actually Promises

The India-New Zealand FTA, negotiated over more than a decade, includes a dedicated mobility provision: a Temporary Employment Entry (TEE) visa pathway allowing up to 5,000 Indian professionals to work in New Zealand for stays of up to three years. The professions covered include IT, engineering, healthcare, and — in a nod to India's cultural exports — AYUSH practitioners and yoga instructors.

The deal also provides uncapped numbers for Indian students, with full work rights during study and after graduation. Officials estimate the agreement could see more than 20,000 Indian migrants entering New Zealand.

Peters and NZ First oppose the deal outright, arguing it gives too much away on immigration without sufficient reciprocity on dairy market access. "National preferred doing a quick, low-quality deal over doing the hard work necessary to get a fair deal that delivers for both New Zealanders and Indians," he said. NZ First has invoked the coalition's "agree to disagree" provision and will vote against the enabling legislation.

The National Party, which leads the coalition, has secured opposition Labour Party support to push the ratification through Parliament. But the simultaneous move to restrict Indian immigration through separate policy settings — even as the FTA promises mobility — strikes many observers as contradictory at best and bad faith at worst.

## A Community Under Pressure

For New Zealand's approximately 250,000-strong Indian diaspora, the developments arrive amid a wider chill. Anti-immigration sentiment has sharpened across the country in recent years, driven by housing pressure, high youth unemployment, and stretched public services.

Far-right figures, including Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki, have staged protests explicitly targeting Indian immigration, holding signs reading "enough is enough" and calling for a freeze on arrivals from India. The movement, while fringe, has grown more visible as the FTA debate has intensified.

The New Zealand government also launched a separate probe into the exploitation of migrant workers from India and Bangladesh — a real and documented problem in sectors like construction, agriculture, and hospitality. But community leaders worry that the exploitation narrative is being weaponised to restrict all Indian migration, rather than to protect the workers themselves.

"There are NZ citizens of Indian race who will face the brunt of this racism," one social media user wrote in a widely shared response to Jones' comments. "Normalising usage of racist slurs like 'butter chicken' is criminal."

## Timing Is Everything

The internal NZ fight lands at an acutely sensitive moment. Modi is expected in New Zealand in the second week of July — the first visit by an Indian Prime Minister in over 40 years. The visit was meant to celebrate the FTA as a milestone in bilateral ties. Instead, it will unfold against the backdrop of a government that signed a trade deal with India while simultaneously writing immigration rules designed to keep Indians out.

India's government has so far been measured in its public response, with the Ministry of External Affairs noting the importance of the bilateral relationship without directly addressing the immigration controversy. But diplomatic sources suggest New Delhi is watching closely, particularly given the India-specific nature of the proposed restrictions.

For NRIs in New Zealand, the message is unsettling: the same government that welcomed Indian trade is not sure it wants Indian people. How Modi navigates this contradiction — publicly or privately — may define whether the FTA delivers on its promise or becomes a symbol of how economic partnerships can coexist with targeted exclusion.

*Sources: Bloomberg via Hindu Business Line, Reuters, BBC World Service, New Zealand Parliament (Hansard), NZ First Party, Dainik Jagran, Inshorts, VisaVerge*
